extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent lawyers, economists, and policy makers interested in patent scope and innovation policy
extracted.subtask_description: A law-review article analyzing the economic effects of patent scope: surveys legal doctrines (enablement, claims, doctrine of equivalents, blocking patents, reverse equivalents, prosecution history estoppel, product/process claims), develops economic models of technical advance, and draws policy implications about claim breadth across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable an invention must meet all the statutory requirements for patentability: novelty, utility, and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are crafted to meet these requirements; enablement and disclosure doctrines operate alongside these statutory requirements during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement (35 U.S.C. §112) / disclosure sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure must be sufficient to enable someone skilled in the relevant art to make and use all the embodiments of the invention encompassed by the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement can be applied loosely: a specification describing one working example may be sufficient; disclosure of an inventive concept or principle can suffice even if not every embodiment is described. Examples: Gillette (conceptual disclosure upheld), Selden (overbroad disclosure narrowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must provide a precise characterization of the 'best mode' of solving the problem the inventor faced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose best mode can invalidate patents (illustrated by a case where a product patent was initially found to infringe but later invalidated for failure to disclose best mode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims define scope (specification vs claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims define the patentee's technological territory (analogous to metes and bounds), while the specification is used to determine patentability and enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims usually encompass more than the material in the specification; courts and examiners treat specification and claims as serving different functions in establishing scope and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue experimentation doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: An alleged infringer may argue noninfringement by showing that extensive experimentation beyond what was disclosed was required to make the allegedly infringing embodiment (i.e., the disclosure requires 'undue experimentation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If disclosure is so vague that no one can tell how to construct the device except by independent experiments, the patent may be void (Edison v. Sawyer & Mann light bulb filament example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on Patent Office examiner for non-enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must point to something in the prior art indicating that some claimed embodiments are impossible or would require additional information; absent such evidence, broad claims may be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office policy places the burden of disproving enablement on the examiner to avoid leaving claim scope to individual examiners' technological forecasting; courts narrow claims later if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of equivalents (function-way-result / Graver Tank test)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no literal infringement, courts ask whether the accused product performs the same function, in substantially the same way, to achieve substantially the same result, and may find infringement under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply after literal infringement question; examples include International Nickel (magnesium equivalence) and Graver Tank formulation; courts stretch claim language 'on proper occasions' after exhaust of interpretive aids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pioneer vs mere-improvement distinction affecting equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts determine the breadth of equivalents in part by whether the patent is a 'pioneer invention' (broad range of equivalents) or a 'mere improvement' (narrower scope of equivalents).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'pioneer patent' covering a wholly novel function or device is 'entitled to a broad range of equivalents'; improvement patents receive less expansive equivalents protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The first step in infringement analysis is to determine whether the challenger’s product falls squarely within the literal language of the patentee’s claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If literal infringement is found, plaintiff succeeds unless defenses (e.g., reverse equivalents) apply; if not, move to equivalents analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalents and new technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: New technologies developed after a patent was issued can constitute equivalents so long as they do not perform a different function or cause the device to operate in a substantially different way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts increasingly find post-issue technologies equivalent (Hughes Aircraft on-board processing example), but this can conflict with enablement principles; caveat: truly meritorious improvements may escape equivalents under reverse equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reverse doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense that a device literally within the claims is nonetheless not infringing because it is 'so far changed in principle' that it performs in a substantially different way and is not an appropriation of the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely used but available (Westinghouse/Boyden brake example; SRI v. Matsushita remanded to consider reverse equivalents); shields significant technical departures even when literal claim language would capture the device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blocking patents / subservient patents and mutual exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Two patents can 'block' each other when a broad patent dominates and a narrower patent claims an improvement; each may require a license from the other to practice the full technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court may declare a patent subservient; although subservient patentees still gain bargaining leverage and can limit dominant patentee damages, blocking patents complicate freedom-to-operate and licensing negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution history estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims or subject matter surrendered during prosecution cannot later be recaptured under the doctrine of equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution history estoppel is a constraint on stretching claim breadth via equivalents; ties allowable equivalents to what was given up during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art limits on stretching claims/equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts are constrained by the prior art when 'stretching' claim language under the doctrine of equivalents; an applicant cannot claim what is in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalents cannot be used to take subject matter lying in the prior art; prior art serves as an outer boundary for permissible claim expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product vs process claims and new-use patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Product claims (composition of matter) are typically broader; a newly discovered use for a known product can often be protected by process claims directed to applying Old Product X to New Application Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dawson Chemical illustrates protecting a new application via a process patent; encourages drafting process claims to capture new uses even when the product itself is unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting purified/natural products (product claims in biotech/chemistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purified versions of naturally occurring products are often claimed as patentable 'new' things when transformed into a useful commercial or therapeutic form, though controversy exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Parke-Davis suggest purified natural products may be patentable; biotechnology cases (Genentech, Scripps/Genentech) show jurisdictional and doctrinal complexity; European Patent Office may reject broad species claims (Leder & Stewart transgenic mammals example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of accused device's merits ('as a whole' test) in equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: The technical merits of an accused device (changes in materials, number/simplicity of components, increased overall efficiency) should be weighed in the equivalents inquiry; cumulative changes may propel the accused device beyond a just scope of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Texas Instruments (hand-held calculator) is instructive: courts applied an 'as a whole' test focusing on substantive technological improvements to deny equivalents; authors suggest using such an analysis as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between enablement and doctrine of equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an inherent tension: enablement suggests limiting claims to what the specification enables, while the doctrine of equivalents permits expanding scope beyond literal claim language; courts sometimes apply equivalents even where enablement would counsel otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note conflict and recommend reconciling doctrines to avoid permitting claim scope beyond what disclosure supports; specific examples show inconsistency across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of incentives and social costs in scope decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent scope decisions affect incentives to develop, license, and improve technologies and have social costs in terms of competition for improvements; scope should be set to balance pioneer's coordination benefits against lost competition for follow-on improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' normative conclusion: without extensively reducing pioneer's incentives, law should at the margin favor a competitive environment for improvements rather than pioneer dominance; policy implications for how courts apply doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement patents and holdup risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement patents encourage bargaining and cross-licensing but can be subject to holdup by the original patentee who may use their dominant patent to capture value from the improver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic outcomes depend on bargaining positions; issuance of improvement patents often mitigates some negative effects but may not eliminate holdup; blocking patents and compulsory licensing history (polyethylene) illustrate practical consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting strategy to capture inventions and new uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants often draft claims broadly (e.g., claiming principle/concept or all non-human transgenic mammals) or draft process claims to protect new uses of known compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad drafting can be allowed during prosecution absent prior-art proof of non-enablement (burden on examiner); courts and EPO may later narrow; examples include Leder & Stewart transgenic mice claims and Rohm & Haas new-use process claim.
